 With daylight saving time ending, your commute can become more hazardous 
 Stream Southern California's News Leader and Original Shows 24/7 By Dominique Newland Wednesday, October 28, 2026 12:24PM Share LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- It's that time of the year again - daylight saving is ending and the clocks will fall back an hour on Nov. 1. That also means the daylight during your commute is about to change.
 When it comes to the morning commute, the time change and the sun's powerful glare can cast a negative light on drivers' ability to see - leading to more crashes.
 "While investigating crashes during those peak commute hours, a lot of drivers do tell me that sunlight played a factor in the crash," said California Highway Patrol Officer Andre Ortiz. "So whether it's wearing your sunglasses, using a sun visor or increasing your following distance and just slowing down, those are all ways we can mitigate bright sunlight and avoid a traffic crash."
 With the sun rising in the east and setting in the west, people heading those directions are impacted the most. Some of the major freeways those commuters may use include the 10, 101 and 60 freeways.
 "Making sure your windshield is clean, both the inside and the outside, because if there's smudges, that glare can be that much worse and may delay that much more reaction time from us," Ortiz added.
 Although we gain an hour of sleep, for evening commuters, the CHP and AAA of Southern California say they see an increase in sleepy drivers when it gets darker earlier.

 "Keep in mind that even though we gain an hour when we fall back, drivers should still be mindful of drowsy driving, especially with the change in your sleep schedule. With darkness arriving earlier, it's really important to stay alert. Get enough sleep and never drive when you're tired," said AAA's Kandace Redd.
